title: Black palm

names.gloss: the green upper part of the black palm tree from which the dilly bag is made
names.note: The dictionary's short gloss 'mangrove' does not match its own definition.

identification.basis: The dictionary glosses duwar as 'black palm', and Roth (1901) records the Bloomfield name du-ar for Drymophloeus normanbyi, now Normanbya normanbyi, the black palm of this region. Anderson (1996) independently names N. normanbyi as the Bloomfield spear and dilly-bag palm.

summary: **[Duwar](word:duwar)** is the black palm (*Normanbya normanbyi*), and also the [spear](entry:spear-and-woomera) made from it [ref:hershberger1982]. This tall, slender rainforest palm grows only in a small stretch of the Wet Tropics, from south of Cooktown to near Mossman, which is Eastern Kuku Yalanji country [ref:rfk-normanbya]. Its trunk gives a very hard, dark timber for spear points and shafts. Its leaf bases give the [fibre](entry:string-and-twine) for **[kakan](word:kakan)**, 'the green upper part of the black palm tree from which the dilly bag is made' [ref:hershberger1982]. Roth recorded both uses on the Bloomfield River around 1900 [ref:roth1901] [ref:roth1904], and Kuku Yalanji weavers still make black-palm [dilly bags](entry:dilly-bags) today [ref:cag-walker].

sections.heading: Names
sections.body:
The dictionary gives **[duwar](word:duwar)** for both 'black palm' and 'black palm spear' [ref:hershberger1982]. Roth wrote the Bloomfield name as *du-ar* and the Cape Bedford (Guugu Yimithirr) name as *do-war*, beside the scientific name of this palm [ref:roth1901]. **[Kakan](word:kakan)** is the green upper part of the palm from which the dilly bag is made [ref:hershberger1982]. The dictionary's one-word English gloss for *[kakan](word:kakan)*, 'mangrove', does not match its own definition and looks like an error. Roth heard the same word on the Bloomfield in 1904. He wrote that baskets or sieve-bags made from this palm 'are known as *karkan*, the name of the plant itself' [ref:roth1904].

Other words grew from the palm. **[Murrangkal](word:murrangkal)** is a 'fighting spear (shovelhead), made from black palm' [ref:hershberger1982]. At Cape Bedford, Roth recorded *mu-rong-al* as a kind of spear 'so called from the timber' of the black palm [ref:roth1901-kyi]. **[Balji](word:balji)** is a 'ladie's dilly bag, made from grass or black palm' [ref:hershberger1982].

sections.heading: Description
sections.body: A single-stemmed palm up to 30 m tall. The trunk is smooth, slender and closely ringed, and **becomes almost black with age** [ref:rfk-normanbya]. The arching leaves are about 2.5 m long, with 75–95 leaflets on each side. Each leaflet is split to the base into 7–11 narrow segments [ref:rfk-normanbya]. The segments are dark green above, silvery beneath and cut off square at the tip like a fishtail, which gives the crown a bushy look like a foxtail palm [ref:wiki-normanbya]. The flower spike, up to 90 cm long, hangs from the trunk just below the leaves. The egg-shaped fruits are 35–50 mm long with a short beak, and ripen **pink to red-brown**. Each holds one large seed with an orange-red coat [ref:rfk-normanbya].

sections.heading: Where it grows
sections.body: Black palm grows in rainforest and vine forest from near sea level to 700 m. It is found only in North East Queensland, **from south of Cooktown to near Mossman** [ref:rfk-normanbya]. More exactly, its range runs from just south of Rossville to just south of the Daintree River [ref:wiki-normanbya].

sections.heading: Uses
sections.body:
**[Spears](entry:spear-and-woomera).** Black palm was the spear wood of the Bloomfield. Anderson lists twelve Kuku Yalanji spear types, and black palm (*N. normanbyi*) is part of almost all of them, either as the handle or as the hardwood point and fore-shaft [ref:anderson1996]. Roth described the *do-war* spear as a long reed shaft with a short black-palm end that 'gives the particular name to the spear', with the 'same name and weapon on the Bloomfield River' [ref:roth1909b13]. The Bloomfield stingray-barbed spears *ta-chal* and *dikara* (the dictionary's **[dajal](word:dajal)** 'fighting spear' and **[dikarra](word:dikarra)** 'war spear, has a stingray barb') had a short [grass-tree](entry:grass-tree) butt and a long black-palm or [bloodwood](entry:bloodwood) shaft [ref:roth1909b13] [ref:hershberger1982]. The hard timber was also split for clapsticks, nulla nullas and [digging sticks](entry:digging-sticks) [ref:wiki-normanbya].

**[Dilly bags](entry:dilly-bags) and sieve-bags.** On the Bloomfield, sieve-bags were made from fibre strands pulled from the leaf bases of the black palm [ref:roth1901-string]. These palm-fibre bags were one of the three main kinds of Kuku Yalanji bag. Women used them to [leach](entry:leaching) [cycad](entry:zamia) flour and to mash and strain the poisonous [hairy yam](entry:yam), and to carry 'anything (including infants)'. A woman's palm-fibre bag was her own and was not lent to others [ref:anderson1996]. Fibre from the crownshaft was also used as [string](entry:string-and-twine) to tie spear heads to shafts, and in [fish traps](entry:fish-traps) and cradles [ref:wiki-normanbya].

**Food.** On the Bloomfield, 'the buds and young leaf-stalks are eaten' [ref:roth1901].

**Troughs.** When better bark was not to hand, dry sheets of black-palm bark could be folded into a temporary trough [ref:anderson1996].

**For animals.** [Cassowaries](entry:cassowary) eat the fruit whole and spread the seed in their droppings [ref:wiki-normanbya].

sections.heading: How it was made
sections.body:
**A black-palm sieve-bag or [dilly bag](entry:dilly-bags) (kakan, balji)**, from Roth's Bloomfield notes and his account of the basket weave [ref:roth1901-string] [ref:roth1904] [ref:anderson1996]:

1. Take the green upper part of the palm, where the leaf stalks clasp the stem [ref:hershberger1982].
2. **Pull the fibre strands out of the leaf bases one at a time.**
3. **Clean each strand by drawing it between the thumb-nail and finger-nail.**
4. Lay out several straight strands as the frame (the 'basal strands' or warp). On the Bloomfield these were **tied together into a bundle** to start the base.
5. Take **two long working strands** and twist them around each frame strand in turn, so that they make a chain. Go around row after row, adding frame strands as the bag widens (Roth's 'chain-twist').
6. Finish the rim. The common methods were **searing the ends in the ashes** or **over-casting** them with another strand [ref:roth1901-string].

**A black-palm [spear](entry:spear-and-woomera) point** [ref:anderson1996] [ref:roth1909b13] [ref:roth1904]:

1. **Split** a length of the hard trunk lengthways [ref:wiki-normanbya].
2. Shape and sharpen the point and fore-shaft, then **harden it in the fire**. The dictionary's *[balnji](word:balnji)* means doing something properly with a fire, 'as in cooking or hardening spears over a fire' [ref:hershberger1982].
3. **Fit the black-palm piece into the long shaft** (reed, bamboo or [grass-tree](entry:grass-tree)).
4. **Bind the joint**, and any [stingray](entry:stingrays) barbs or extra prongs, with [wallaby](entry:wallaby) [sinew](entry:sinew).
5. **Seal the binding with hot resin.** Use brown cedar (*Canarium*) gum, [Cooktown ironwood](entry:ironwood) root gum or grass-tree resin (**[kanunjul](word:kanunjul)**). Smooth it with a small greased wooden board. Roth saw this tool in use on the Bloomfield [ref:roth1904].
6. Spear handles were usually painted with **red and white stripes** [ref:anderson1996].

sections.heading: Safety
sections.body: Black palm is single-stemmed [ref:rfk-normanbya], so cutting out the bud for food or the crown for fibre ends that palm. The species is listed as **Vulnerable** by the IUCN because of land clearing, though Queensland rates it Least Concern [ref:wiki-normanbya]. Take only what is needed, with the right people's permission. Leave the fallen fruit for the [cassowaries](entry:cassowary), which spread its seed [ref:wiki-normanbya]. Fire-hardened black-palm [spears](entry:spear-and-woomera) are real weapons and should be handled as such [ref:anderson1996].

sections.heading: On Country today
sections.body: Almost the whole range of the black palm lies inside the Wet Tropics World Heritage Area [ref:wiki-normanbya]. Some privately owned lowland rainforest still has an uncertain future [ref:wiki-normanbya]. Native title holders may gather for personal, domestic and communal needs without permits under s 211 of the *Native Title Act 1993* [ref:alrc-s211]. Visitors need Traditional Owners' permission to cut or collect, and park rules apply.

sections.heading: Language
sections.body: **[duwar](word:duwar)** 'black palm; black palm spear'; **[kakan](word:kakan)** black palm top for dilly bags; **[balji](word:balji)** woman's dilly bag; **[ngunyin](word:ngunyin)** '[dilly bag](entry:dilly-bags)'; **[murrangkal](word:murrangkal)** shovel-headed fighting spear of black palm; **[dajal](word:dajal)** 'fighting spear'; **[dikarra](word:dikarra)** stingray-barbed war spear; **[kalka](word:kalka)** 'fishing spear, also generic term for [spear](entry:spear-and-woomera)'; **[kanunjul](word:kanunjul)** [grass-tree](entry:grass-tree) resin 'used to make pitch to seal spear bindings' [ref:hershberger1982].

locations.summary: **Black palm does not grow on the Hann.** It is a rainforest palm found only 'from south of Cooktown to near Mossman', and the Atlas of Living Australia has no record of it in a box of about 90 × 85 km around the middle Hann, Laura and western Rinyirru [ref:rfk-normanbya] [ref:ala-hann-palm]. Its wood reached this side of the range only by trade: black-palm spear wood was bartered from the McIvor River as far as Princess Charlotte Bay [ref:roth1909b13].

sections.heading: The palms of this country
sections.body: The palms here are the fan palms. In Rinyirru 'scattered communities of Corypha and fan palms occur in alluvial areas, alongside the rivers and creeks' [ref:qpws-rinyirru-2013]. In 1872 William Hann, camped on the North Kennedy at what is now Hann Crossing, wrote: 'Close to our camp were clumps of fan palms of immense beauty' [ref:qpws-rinyirru-culture].

sections.heading: Spears in this country
sections.body: No published record says how the Possum or Thaypan people used traded black-palm wood. Around 1900 the spears moving through the Princess Charlotte Bay trade were others: the Koko-rarmul of the Morehead River gave the Koko-warra 'reed-spears, iron-scraps, European tomahawks, etc.', and the Endeavour and Bloomfield people supplied the Koko-warra with 'red-ochre, white-clay, grass-tree spears, etc.' [ref:roth1910b14]. See [spear and woomera](entry:spear-and-woomera).

locations.summary: Black palm does not grow in Western Yalanji country; on the upper Mitchell it was known through trade, if at all [ref:rfk-normanbya] [ref:roth1910b14].

sections.heading: Not here
sections.body: The palm does not grow in the dry open woodland of the Mitchell and Palmer rivers [ref:rfk-normanbya]. Its products did travel, though. The Bloomfield people traded [dilly-bags](entry:dilly-bags) and [spears](entry:spear-and-woomera) with their neighbours [ref:roth1910b14], and black-palm spear wood was bartered from the McIvor River as far as Princess Charlotte Bay [ref:roth1909b13].

locations.summary: This is black-palm country: the palm grows nowhere else, and the Bloomfield's spears and bags were made from it [ref:rfk-normanbya] [ref:anderson1996].

sections.heading: Where it grows here
sections.body: The palm's range is the rainforest heart of Eastern Kuku Yalanji country, the Daintree, Cape Tribulation and Bloomfield. Kuku Yalanji weaver Delissa Walker gathers it in the Daintree rainforest around Cow Bay [ref:cag-walker].

sections.heading: Made here
sections.body: Louisa Smith was photographed making a *[balji](word:balji)* this way with black palm fibre at Wujal Wujal in 1982 [ref:anderson1996].

sections.heading: On country today
sections.body:
Much of it is now Eastern Kuku Yalanji land. The Daintree, Ngalba-bulal, Kalkajaka and Hope Islands national parks were handed back on 29 September 2021 and are jointly managed with the Queensland Government [ref:qld-handback].

The weaving lives on. Delissa Walker learnt traditional **[kakan](word:kakan)** basket weaving from her grandmother, Ngadijina Wilma Walker. She is one of very few weavers still using black palm. Her *Kakan (dilly bag)* works of black palm and [lawyer cane](entry:lawyer-cane) (2017) are held by Cairns Art Gallery [ref:cag-walker].
